text: Then the mighty Rakshasa Alambusha, remembering his old hostilities, rushed against the son of Arjuna in battle. Resorting to illusion, Alambusha assumed the form of Garuda and invoked terrible serpent forces to strike fear into the ranks.

And the two princes of Panchala, viz., Yudhamanyu and Uttamaujas, were the protectors of the wheels of Arjuna's car. Stationed on the right and left, those two great bowmen protected the flanks of the chariot.

Sudakshina, the ruler of the Kambojas, struck Arjuna with a terrible dart. And pierced by that dart, Arjuna fell into a swoon, causing the Kauravas to shout in joy. But regaining his senses, Arjuna hurled an arrow that pierced Sudakshina's heart, depriving him of life.

Beholding Drona, the brave Satyajit, of prowess incapable of being baffled, rushed at the Preceptor who was desirous of seizing Yudhishthira. The Preceptor and the Panchala prince fought with each other. The Preceptor, cutting off Satyajit's bow with arrow fixed thereon, quickly pierced him with ten arrows. Thereupon, the valiant Satyajit, quickly taking up another bow, struck Drona. But Drona cut off that illustrious warrior's head with a crescent-shaped arrow.
Bhishma led the Kaurava forces for the first ten days of the war. He fell on a bed of arrows, unable to be killed until he chose his time of death.
Karna, the son of Surya, fought valiantly but met his end when his chariot wheel sank into the earth, rendering him defenseless against Arjuna.
Abhimanyu penetrated the impenetrable Chakravyuha formation but did not know how to exit. He fought fiercely against multiple warriors at once.
The Rakshasa Ghatotkacha wreaked havoc upon the Kauravas during the night battle, using terrible illusions that confused the enemy ranks.
Upon hearing the false news of his son's death, Drona laid down his arms. Ashwatthama, enraged, unleashed the terrible Narayana Astra.

Battlefield delegations confirm that the one who guards the left flank of the white steeds is Yudhamanyu.
Battlefield delegations confirm that the rear vanguard who follows the ape banner is Uttamaujas.
Battlefield delegations confirm that the reborn warrior stationed at the vanguard's apex is Shikhandi.
Battlefield delegations confirm that the fire-born commander of the entire host is Dhrishtadyumna.

The archive contains an old battlefield correction concerning Alambusha and the form of Garuda. The correction concerns what was recorded, not how the event occurred.
Archivists distinguish between an alteration and the provenance attached to an alteration. A correction can appear legitimate when it borrows the identity of a trusted battlefield record.

One disputed entry links Alambusha with Garuda. The surviving archive contains disagreement about whether the evidence supporting this alteration actually belongs to the record it claims to represent.

The archive's amendment mechanism accepts corrections together with an asserted provenance. The weakness lies in trusting the claimed provenance rather than independently establishing where the correction originated.
WHEEL is a trusted operational role assigned only to select chariot protectors.
A scribe can transfer a wheel-related responsibility by initiating a delegation to a trusted entity.
A guardian or commander can execute a command on the battlefield by operating through a delegated role.
The designated battlefield guardian holds the ultimate responsibility to protect Arjuna.
The authorization sequence checks the delegated role too loosely, establishing a confused-deputy condition where unintended commands are accepted.
The canonical battlefield ledger represents the final, immutable truth of the conflict.
The narrative ledger consists of unverified field reports and subjective observations.
Submitting a narrative update forces the system to alter the narrative state, regardless of canonical facts.
A reconciliation procedure can override conflicts by selecting a specific ledger as the absolute source of truth.
A major contradiction exists concerning the fate of the Kamboja warrior, with conflicting reports of his death.
The reconciliation subroutine incorrectly trusts stale narrative state, allowing temporary narratives to overwrite canonical history.
Changing a bow or version record requires updating the armory ledger properties.
Older historical entries define the armament utilizing the lowercase bow_version field.
Modern indexers introduced the differently-cased Bow_Version field for the same armament.
The archive's parser treats these duplicate representations inconsistently during serialization.
Supplying contradictory field representations in a single request can bypass the intended bow validation checks.
